title: Recommendation Systems
description: Compare collaborative filtering, content-based, and hybrid approaches. Study Netflix Prize insights, YouTube's deep neural network architecture, and cold start solutions.

segments.text: Recommendations drive thirty-five percent of Amazon's revenue and eighty percent of Netflix viewing. A one percent improvement in recommendation quality translates to millions in revenue. The Netflix Prize — a one-million-dollar competition for ten percent accuracy improvement — attracted over forty thousand teams and advanced the field by a decade. This is the most commercially valuable ML problem.

Collaborative filtering: users who liked similar items will like similar future items. User-user: find users similar to you, recommend what they liked. Item-item: find items similar to what you liked, recommend those. Matrix factorization decomposes the user-item interaction matrix into latent factors — each user and item gets a vector, the dot product predicts the rating.

Content-based filtering uses item features — genre, director, keywords — to recommend similar items. If you watched three sci-fi movies, recommend more sci-fi. No cold start for items — new items with metadata can be recommended immediately. But it creates filter bubbles — you'll never discover comedy if you only watched sci-fi. And it can't capture taste nuances that aren't in metadata.

Hybrid approaches combine collaborative and content-based. Netflix uses a cascade: candidate generation with collaborative filtering produces a few hundred candidates, then a ranking model using content features, user features, and contextual features scores and orders them. This gives the breadth of collaborative filtering with the precision of content-based ranking.

A brand new user signs up for your streaming service. They have zero watch history. Collaborative filtering fails completely — no data to find similar users. Content-based also fails — no interaction data. How do you make good recommendations for a new user?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you solve the cold start problem for a new user with zero interaction history?

segments.text: Cold start solutions: ask users to rate a few items during onboarding — Netflix shows a taste survey. Use demographic signals — age, location, language — to match with similar demographic clusters. Show globally popular items as a baseline. For new items: use content features and promote new items to a small percentage of users to gather initial feedback rapidly.

YouTube's recommendation system uses a two-tower deep neural network. The candidate generation tower processes hundreds of millions of videos through an embedding model, selecting hundreds of candidates. The ranking tower uses a deep network with video features, user features, and context — time of day, device, watch history — to score and rank the final set of twenty to fifty recommendations.

Recommendation metrics go beyond accuracy. Precision at K: how many of the top K recommendations are relevant. Recall: what fraction of relevant items are recommended. Diversity: are recommendations varied or repetitive. Novelty: are recommendations surprising or obvious. Optimize for engagement but monitor for diversity — pure engagement optimization leads to clickbait and addiction.

Real-time recommendation updates respond to immediate user behavior. User starts watching a thriller — immediately adjust recommendations to include more thrillers. This requires feature computation in real-time and model inference on updated features. Netflix updates recommendation context within seconds of user actions using a real-time feature pipeline feeding into pre-computed candidate sets.

Design a recommendation system for an e-commerce platform with ten million products and one hundred million users. Requirements: sub-one-hundred-millisecond latency, handle cold start, and support real-time personalization. What's your architecture?
segments.thought_prompt: Design recommendations for 10M products, 100M users, sub-100ms latency with cold start handling.

segments.text: Recommendation systems combine collaborative filtering for discovering taste patterns, content-based filtering for item understanding, and deep learning for ranking precision. The cascade architecture — generate candidates then rank — scales to billions of items. Solve cold start with onboarding surveys and demographics. And always balance engagement optimization with diversity to avoid filter bubbles.
